slides.title: Hodgkin-Huxley: the equations of the action potential
slides.body:
**Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) model** (1952): the first quantitative biophysical theory of an excitable membrane, derived from voltage-clamp experiments on the squid giant axon. Four coupled ODEs, three gating variables (m, h, n), one voltage (V) — they fit + predicted the action potential's shape, threshold, refractory period, and propagation velocity to within experimental error. Hodgkin + Huxley shared the 1963 Nobel in Physiology or Medicine with John Eccles (synaptic IPSPs/EPSPs). The HH formalism is still the foundation of every modern neural simulator (NEURON, GENESIS, Brian, NEST, the Allen + Blue Brain detailed models).

**The system** (per unit area):

  C_m · dV/dt = -[ g_Na · m³ · h · (V - E_Na) + g_K · n⁴ · (V - E_K) + g_L · (V - E_L) ] + I_stim

  dm/dt = α_m(V)·(1-m) - β_m(V)·m
  dh/dt = α_h(V)·(1-h) - β_h(V)·h
  dn/dt = α_n(V)·(1-n) - β_n(V)·n

**Interpretation**:
- **m** = Na⁺ activation gate (3 independent subunits → m³); fast (~0.1 ms).
- **h** = Na⁺ inactivation gate (one subunit, h); slower (~1 ms). Channel open only when m³h ≈ 1.
- **n** = K⁺ activation gate (4 subunits → n⁴); slower than m, faster than h. Delayed-rectifier K⁺ has no inactivation in original HH.
- **g_Na ≈ 120 mS/cm²**, **g_K ≈ 36 mS/cm²**, **g_L ≈ 0.3 mS/cm²**; **E_Na ≈ +60**, **E_K ≈ -90**, **E_L ≈ -54 mV**; **C_m ≈ 1 µF/cm²**.

**Threshold + all-or-none**: subthreshold depolarization decays passively. Above ~-55 mV the regenerative positive feedback (more depolarization → more Na⁺ activation → more depolarization) launches the spike. Once triggered, amplitude (~100 mV) is independent of stimulus strength — the AP is digital.

**Refractory period**:
- **Absolute** (~1-2 ms): h ≈ 0 (Na⁺ inactivated); no second spike possible regardless of stimulus.
- **Relative** (~5-10 ms): h partially recovered + n still elevated (K⁺ still flowing); larger stimulus needed.
- Sets maximum firing rate ~500-1000 Hz for fast spikers (PV interneurons; auditory MNTB).

**Saltatory conduction**: in myelinated axons, depolarization 'jumps' between **nodes of Ranvier** (Ranvier 1878) where Nav channels cluster at >1000/µm². Internodal myelin (~100 wraps of oligodendrocyte/Schwann membrane) raises R_m + lowers C_m, boosting passive propagation. Speeds: unmyelinated C-fibers ~1 m/s; large myelinated Aα motor + Ia afferent ~120 m/s.

**Cable equation** (Rall 1959+): treats the dendrite/axon as a leaky cable: ∂V/∂t = (λ²/τ)·∂²V/∂x² - V/τ + I/c. Length constant λ governs passive spread (~100-1000 µm); compartmental models discretize Rall's equations + couple HH dynamics per segment. Wilfrid Rall pioneered dendritic computation theory before structural data existed.

slides.title: Voltage-clamp history: from squid to Nobel
slides.body:
**The squid giant axon** (Young 1936): up to 1 mm diameter; supplied to mantle's stellate ganglion for fast jet escape; large enough to thread electrodes inside — the experimental workhorse of mid-20th-century neurophysiology. Marine Biological Laboratory at Plymouth (UK) + Woods Hole (US) were the centers.

**Cole + Curtis (1939)**: at Woods Hole, used a Wheatstone-bridge impedance method on the squid axon. Showed the membrane's capacitance stayed nearly constant during an action potential while membrane resistance dropped ~40-fold — proving that the AP is a transient permeability change, not a breakdown of the membrane. The conceptual foundation HH built on.

**Hodgkin, Huxley + Katz at Plymouth, 1939**: just before WWII, recorded the first intracellular AP from the squid axon, showing overshoot (V briefly exceeds 0 mV) — incompatible with Bernstein's 1902 'K⁺ short-circuit' theory + suggesting active Na⁺ influx. War interrupted; Hodgkin worked on radar.

**Voltage clamp** (Marmont + Cole 1949; refined by Hodgkin + Huxley + Katz 1949-52): a feedback amplifier holds V at a commanded value while measuring the current needed to do so — separating channel currents from capacitive currents. Stepping V exposes the kinetics of g_Na + g_K independently. Without voltage clamp the system is too tangled to dissect.

**The 1952 J. Physiol papers** — five back-to-back papers, the cornerstone of modern biophysics:
- (a) Hodgkin, Huxley, Katz: measurement of current-voltage relations.
- (b) Hodgkin + Huxley: components of membrane current.
- (c) Hodgkin + Huxley: dual effect of membrane potential on sodium conductance.
- (d) Hodgkin + Huxley: kinetics + steady-state properties of potassium conductance.
- (e) Hodgkin + Huxley: **quantitative description of membrane current + its application to conduction + excitation in nerve** — the master synthesis with the HH equations + numerical integration (by hand crank calculator) reproducing the AP.

**Nobel 1963**: Hodgkin + Huxley shared with John Carew Eccles, who had discovered IPSPs + EPSPs in spinal motor neurons. The HH model converted neurophysiology from descriptive to quantitative — what Newton did for mechanics, HH did for the neuron.

**Subsequent milestones**:
- **Patch clamp** (Neher + Sakmann 1976; Nobel 1991): record single channels at pA + ms resolution; confirms HH's gating-variable interpretation as discrete channel openings.
- **Channel cloning** (Numa et al. 1984 nAChR; 1986 Nav; 1987 Kv): cDNA sequences reveal 4-domain Nav, 4-subunit Kv, the molecular reality behind m, h, n.
- **Crystal structures** (MacKinnon Kv structure 1998 → Nobel Chemistry 2003): pore + selectivity filter (TVGYG signature in K⁺ channels) + voltage sensor (S4 helices with arginines).

**Hodgkin-Huxley** stands as a model of physical biology: from impedance measurements (1939) to a 4-ODE system (1952) to Nobel (1963) to atomic structure (1998+) to the brain-scale simulators (2010s+) — all unified by the equations on the previous slide.

slides.title: Channel pharmacology + channelopathies
slides.body:
**Voltage-gated channels** are validated drug targets — antiarrhythmics, anticonvulsants, local anesthetics, analgesics, and many natural toxins exploit them.

**Sodium channels (Nav1.1-Nav1.9)** — α-subunits encoded by SCN1A-SCN11A; β-subunits modulate:
- **TTX (tetrodotoxin)** from pufferfish + Pacific newts: blocks Nav pore from extracellular side at nM affinity; the prototypical pharmacological 'OFF' switch. Nav1.5 (cardiac) + Nav1.8/1.9 (DRG) are TTX-resistant. Furikake-grade poisoning has no antidote.
- **STX (saxitoxin)** from dinoflagellates (red tide): similar mechanism; cause of paralytic shellfish poisoning.
- **Lidocaine, procaine, bupivacaine**: local anesthetics; state-dependent block (preferentially bind inactivated Nav), explaining use-dependence + selectivity for high-firing nociceptors.
- **Phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide**: anticonvulsants; state-dependent Nav block reduces burst firing in epileptic foci.
- **Class I antiarrhythmics** (quinidine, flecainide): cardiac Nav1.5 block; treat ventricular arrhythmias.
- **Veratridine, batrachotoxin** (poison-dart frog): hold Nav open — toxic.

**Potassium channels (Kv1-Kv12)** — vast family:
- **TEA (tetraethylammonium)**: classic Kv blocker; used by HH to isolate g_Na.
- **4-AP (4-aminopyridine)**: Kv1 blocker; clinical use in MS (Ampyra/Fampridine) to improve nerve conduction.
- **Apamin** (bee venom): blocks SK Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channels.
- **α-Dendrotoxin** (mamba): Kv1 blocker.
- **Sulfonylureas** (glibenclamide): close pancreatic K_ATP → depolarize β-cells → insulin release; oral antidiabetics.

**Calcium channels (Cav1-Cav3)**:
- **L-type (Cav1)** dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine): antihypertensives; verapamil/diltiazem class IV antiarrhythmics.
- **N-type (Cav2.2)**: ω-conotoxin MVIIA = **ziconotide** (Prialt) intrathecal for chronic pain.
- **T-type (Cav3)**: ethosuximide for absence epilepsy.

**Channelopathies** — diseases of ion channels:
- **Dravet syndrome**: SCN1A loss-of-function in PV interneurons; severe pediatric epilepsy. Catastrophic; some response to cannabidiol + fenfluramine.
- **Long QT syndrome (LQT1)**: KCNQ1 (Kv7.1) loss of function; delayed cardiac repolarization → torsades de pointes → sudden death.
- **LQT2**: KCNH2 (hERG); also acquired drug-induced LQT (cisapride, terfenadine pulled).
- **LQT3**: SCN5A gain of function.
- **Episodic ataxia type 2**: CACNA1A (Cav2.1) loss; spinocerebellar ataxia 6 = expansion of same gene.
- **Familial hemiplegic migraine 1**: CACNA1A gain.
- **Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis**: SCN4A.
- **Cystic fibrosis**: CFTR (Cl⁻ channel; ABC transporter family) — not voltage-gated but the most common channelopathy; modulators (ivacaftor, elexacaftor) revolutionized therapy.
- **Brugada syndrome**: SCN5A loss; ST elevation + sudden death.
- **Erythromelalgia + paroxysmal extreme pain disorder**: Nav1.7 (SCN9A) gain; congenital insensitivity to pain = Nav1.7 loss (Cox 2006 Pakistani pedigree) → Nav1.7 antagonists are intense pain-drug targets.
- **Myasthenia gravis** (autoantibody to nAChR), **Lambert-Eaton** (anti-Cav2.1): autoimmune channelopathies.

**Channel-state-dependent design**: modern anticonvulsants + antiarrhythmics + analgesics increasingly exploit selectivity for inactivated states + tissue-specific channel isoforms — minimizing off-target effects. Cryo-EM structures of Nav, Kv, Cav, TRP, CFTR have opened structure-based design pipelines (Catterall, MacKinnon, Yan, Hite, Hilgemann labs).

question.question: Derive a simplified HH-style AP
question.goal: Starting from V = -65 mV at rest, walk through the four phases of a single AP, naming the dominant currents + gating-variable values at each stage.

steps.prompt: Rest. What are m, h, n + dominant current?

acceptedAnswers: m ~0.05, h ~0.6, n ~0.3; leak K⁺ dominant

hints: Steady-state values at V_rest from α/β curves.
steps.reveal: At V_rest ≈ -65 mV: m_∞ ≈ 0.05 (Na activation low), h_∞ ≈ 0.6 (most Na not yet inactivated), n_∞ ≈ 0.3 (some K open). Total g_Na = 120·m³·h ≈ 0.001 mS/cm² (negligible); g_K = 36·n⁴ ≈ 0.3 mS/cm²; g_L = 0.3. Leak + small K⁺ set V_rest. Pump runs in background restoring gradients.

steps.prompt: Upstroke. Stimulus pushes V past threshold (~-55 mV). What happens?

acceptedAnswers: m → 1 fast (~0.1 ms); g_Na rises ~500-fold; V rushes toward E_Na = +60 mV

hints: m responds to V on sub-ms timescale; positive feedback.
steps.reveal: Depolarization sharply raises α_m → m approaches m_∞(V) ≈ 1 with τ_m ~0.1 ms. m³ rises ~8000-fold; g_Na can exceed 100 mS/cm². Inward Na⁺ current (I_Na = g_Na·(V - E_Na)) further depolarizes → more activation → runaway upstroke at dV/dt up to 500 V/s in fast axons. V overshoots toward +30 to +40 mV (never quite E_Na = +60 because K⁺ catches up).

steps.prompt: Repolarization. What turns off Na⁺ + brings V down?

acceptedAnswers: h → 0 (Na inactivates); n → 1 (K⁺ activates); outward I_K dominates

hints: h has slower kinetics than m; n is delayed.
steps.reveal: Two processes terminate the spike: (1) Na⁺ inactivation — h decays toward h_∞(V_peak) ≈ 0 with τ_h ~1 ms, shutting Na⁺ off; (2) delayed-rectifier K⁺ — n rises toward n_∞ ≈ 1 with τ_n ~1-5 ms, opening g_K to ~30 mS/cm². Net current becomes strongly outward, V plummets toward E_K = -90 mV.

acceptedAnswers: n still elevated → V below rest; h slow to recover → absolute then relative refractory

hints: n stays high after V repolarizes; h recovers slowly at hyperpolarized V.
steps.reveal: Briefly after repolarization n remains elevated, holding V near E_K (AHP ~5-10 mV below rest, lasting ~5-10 ms). Meanwhile h recovers from inactivation only at hyperpolarized potentials with τ ~5 ms. While h ≈ 0, no AP is possible regardless of stimulus (absolute refractory). As h partially recovers + n decays, a stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire (relative refractory). Sets maximum firing rate (~500 Hz cortical PV; ~1 kHz auditory).

question.question: Why does the Hodgkin-Huxley model use m³h for Na⁺ and n⁴ for K⁺ conductance?
options: HH fit empirical voltage-clamp current traces and found that Na⁺ activation rose with a delayed sigmoidal shape best modeled as three independent gating particles in series (m³), each obeying first-order kinetics, while Na⁺ inactivation overlaid a single particle (h). K⁺ activation fit a steeper sigmoid best modeled as four particles (n⁴). The exponents were chosen by curve-fitting — HH did not know the molecular basis. Decades later, channel cloning (Numa, Catterall, Jan, MacKinnon) showed Kv channels are tetramers (4 identical α-subunits) and Nav channels are pseudo-tetramers (4 homologous domains of one polypeptide) — each subunit/domain contributes one S4 voltage sensor — beautifully validating m, h, n as physical entities. MacKinnon's 1998 KcsA + 2002 Kv crystal structures (Nobel Chemistry 2003) cemented the picture. HH's empirical fit reflected real molecular architecture decades before it was visualized.
question.explanation: HH's m³h + n⁴ were empirical fits to voltage-clamp data. Later channel cloning (Numa 1984+) + crystal structures (MacKinnon Kv 1998, Nobel 2003) revealed Kv channels are tetramers + Nav are pseudo-tetramers — 4 voltage sensors each — validating the exponents as physical subunit counts. The 1952 equations encoded real molecular architecture decades before it was visualized.

hints: Channel structure later validated the exponents.
slides.workedSolution: m³h + n⁴ came from curve-fitting voltage-clamp data: 3 + 1 + 4 'gating particles' captured kinetics. Channel cloning (Numa 1984+) + crystal structures (MacKinnon Kv 1998, Nobel Chemistry 2003) showed Kv = tetramer, Nav = pseudo-tetramer with 4 S4 voltage sensors — confirming m, h, n as physical molecular entities. The empirical exponents reflected real architecture decades before it was visualized.

question.question: A novel mutation in SCN1A causes Nav1.1 channels to recover from inactivation 2x slower (τ_h doubled at hyperpolarized V).
question.prompt: Predict the effect on PV-interneuron firing rates and downstream cortical excitability. Why does this cause Dravet syndrome's catastrophic epilepsy? Tie to interneuron-driven gamma oscillations + the failure mode (loss of inhibition rather than excess excitation). What would you screen for in zebrafish + iPSC-derived neurons?

question.question: Write the HH membrane equation (in terms of g_Na, g_K, g_L, m, h, n, V, and reversal potentials).
acceptedAnswers: C_m dV/dt = -g_Na m^3 h (V - E_Na) - g_K n^4 (V - E_K) - g_L (V - E_L) + I_stim
question.hint: Capacitive current = sum of ionic currents (with sign) + stimulus.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why Hodgkin-Huxley is considered the founding model of quantitative neuroscience.
question.rubric: Mentions: HH (1952) was the first quantitative biophysical theory of an excitable membrane — four ODEs (V + m, h, n) parameterized from voltage-clamp data on the squid giant axon predicted AP shape, threshold, refractory period + propagation velocity. Nobel 1963 (with Eccles). The framework was empirically derived (m³h + n⁴ as curve-fits) but turned out to encode real molecular architecture: K channels are tetramers, Na channels are pseudo-tetramers with 4 S4 voltage sensors — confirmed by Numa cloning (1980s) + MacKinnon structures (Nobel 2003). HH remains the substrate of modern simulators (NEURON, GENESIS, Brian, NEST, Allen + Blue Brain) + the conceptual frame for understanding channelopathies (Dravet, LQT, episodic ataxia) + pharmacology (TTX, lidocaine, anticonvulsants). It is to neuroscience what Newton's laws are to mechanics: a small set of equations from which most observed dynamics can be derived.
